# Peer-to-Peer Mental Health Training: A National Model for Peer Support for Medical and Dental Students

**Authors:** Armand Amini; Avina Rami; Rhea W. Teng; Clara Baselga-Garriga; Kaiz Esmail; Marium Raza; William Oles; Ivo H. Cerda; Mark É. Czeisler; Mariel T. Sander; Vivian Wang; Surya Pulukuri; David Abramson; Fidencio Saldaña; Jennifer Potter

**Affiliations:** 1 Fourth-Year Medical Student, Harvard Medical School | 2 Second-Year Medical Student, Harvard Medical School | 3 Psychiatrist, Harvard University Health Services; Director, Counseling and Mental Health Service, Longwood Medical Clinic, Harvard University | 4 Assistant Professor, Department of Medicine, Harvard Medical School; Dean for Students, Harvard Medical School | 5 Professor, Department of Medicine, Harvard Medical School; Advisory Dean, Castle Society, Harvard Medical School

## Abstract

Medical and dental students experience higher-than-average prevalence of depression, anxiety, burnout, and suicidal ideation compared to the age-matched general population. Early interventions for these students can prevent escalation to more acute mental health crises and suicide. Studies show that medical students first seek support from their peers. Our curriculum teaches students how to support both themselves and their peers prior to an acute mental health crisis.

The authors designed, implemented, and evaluated a 90-minute peer-to-peer mental health training that aimed to equip first-year medical and dental students with skills and resources to intervene on behalf of a peer experiencing mental health distress. The workshop consisted of a peer-led didactic session, dyad role-play sessions, and a guided reflection. Resources included a slide deck, student handouts detailing the dyad role-plays, and pre/postsession surveys.

One hundred sixty-four first-year students from Harvard Medical School and Harvard School of Dental Medicine completed the required training. Comparisons of survey responses by paired t tests indicated statistically significant increases in mean scores for eight items assessing learner confidence, and an increased sum score of six items assessing learner knowledge (mean of 5.6 postsession vs. 5.4 presession; p = .04).

Our results demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of peer-led mental health training to increase first-year medical and dental students’ related knowledge and confidence in identifying and responding to peers experiencing emotional distress. The resources developed for this training can be adapted to provide foundational mental health training at other medical and dental institutions.

## Educational Objectives

By the end of this activity, learners will be able to: 1.Explain the importance of peer mental health awareness in medical education.2.Identify signs and symptoms of peer mental health distress.3.Respond appropriately to a distressed peer in a simulated interaction.4.Utilize the curricular tools provided to facilitate future peer mental health training.

## Introduction

Medical and dental students experience higher-than-average prevalence of depression, anxiety, burnout, and suicidal ideation when compared to the age-matched general population.1–4 Transitioning to medical and dental school brings numerous stressors, including frequent examinations, performance pressure, and exposure to emotionally salient patient encounters, suffering, and death.5,6 Compared to other graduate students, medical students are particularly vulnerable to depression and anxiety due to their routine exposure to illness and mortality.7 While formal mental health infrastructures are imperative, studies show that medical students often seek support from their peers to handle these stressors.8–10

Peer-teaching models offer an opportunity to address mental health concerns in medical students. These models, widely used in undergraduate medical education, are supported by the theory that peers who share experiences with their learners can be effective educators.11 While peer-led initiatives in medical school are abundant, especially pertaining to clinical development, few of them focus on addressing medical student mental health. Of the more than 300 publications yielded from a keyword search for mental health in MedEdPORTAL, only five focus on the mental health or well-being of medical students,12–16 and only one describes a peer-to-peer training approach. Moreover, these curricula focus on crisis response rather than early identification of mental health challenges. Similarly, a keyword search on PubMed for mental health medical students peer to peer yielded 450 results, of which only five publications described peer-to-peer support programs for medical students.17–21

While college peer-to-peer mental health support programs have demonstrated efficacy,22 the existing studies examining peer education for mental health support among medical students have yielded mixed results due to program and measure heterogeneity.18,23 A meta-analysis exploring peer support in addressing student mental health services found only 28 reports addressing this issue, and most of them were rated poor or fair in their risk of bias.23 A randomized controlled study in New Zealand found that participants who received a peer-led mental health–focused intervention showed improvements, but these changes did not reach statistical significance.18

To determine the efficacy of peer-led mental health support, a group of first-year medical and dental students launched the Harvard Medical School/Harvard School of Dental Medicine (HMS/HSDM) Student Mental Health Task Force in 2022 to establish, with administrative support and mentorship, a peer-support training in the first-year curriculum. The training was adapted, with permission, from a successful program developed for college students by one of the task force leaders and colleagues at the University of Southern California. Following Kern's model for curriculum development,24 we conducted a needs assessment through a class-wide survey (see further details in Methods), which demonstrated that approximately one-half of the students surveyed were interested in receiving peer-to-peer mental health education.16

## Methods

### Curriculum Development and Pilot Training

Among first-year medical and dental students at HMS/HSDM during the 2021–2022 academic year, we observed peers facing significant mental health challenges. These observations were underscored by a class-wide survey that revealed a high prevalence of depression, anxiety, and feelings of intense hopelessness, fueled in part by limited professional support and the COVID-19 pandemic. This survey also revealed that many HMS/HSDM students had reached out to their peers for support, a phenomenon supported by prior research.

In February 2022, eight students on the HMS/HSDM Student Mental Health Task Force began outlining a mental health training program for incoming medical and dental students to enhance confidence in identifying peer distress and offering appropriate support. With input from the medical school administration, including psychiatric specialists from Harvard University Health Services (HUHS), the three-part training (see details under Training Implementation) was created.

After approval of the training materials by the group's faculty advisor and the psychiatric subspecialist from HUHS, we launched a pilot 90-minute session during Professional Development Week 1, an HMS/HSDM course on professional identity formation. The peer-led sessions, held in small groups, were assessed using pre- and postsession surveys to assess learner knowledge, confidence, and overall experience. Results showed increased confidence in all areas and improvement on all knowledge questions, except self-care. Free responses reflected that the session was effective in filling gaps in the curriculum, supported the peer-to-peer model, and confirmed that the session should be required for the whole class. Training content was further refined using pilot feedback, a subsequent optional pilot training session, and a presentation of pilot results at the 2023 AAMC Annual Meeting, prior to the implementation of the required training for all students in March 2024.

### Peer Leader Selection and Preparation

All HMS/HSDM students were invited to apply as peer leaders a month before the training launch. Nine students were selected by two senior peer leaders who facilitated the pilot sessions and mentored the new leaders throughout. Each student had an interest in mental health education, with varying levels of experience with facilitating previous mental health trainings.

Peer leaders attended an introductory orientation and a virtual, mandatory train-the-trainer session on leading small-group discussions, which included a review of training content and logistics with a senior peer leader. All peer leaders received a recording of the session for review (Appendix A—recording begins after introductions and stops before a brief logistical wrap-up; multiple topics covered are institution-specific, and guidance on how to adapt the training at new institutions is included in Appendix B) and met one-on-one virtually with a senior peer leader to practice delivering the presentation. Leaders were encouraged to personalize their sessions while ensuring all core information was covered.

### Training Implementation

The 90-minute training (Appendix C—PowerPoint presentation including speaker notes) was delivered in March 2024 as part of the required Professional Development Week 1 course. Nine peer leaders facilitated in-person small groups of 15–20 students (one group led by two peer leaders). Sessions began with introductions and the administration of a presession survey. Following a trauma-informed approach, students were reminded they could participate at their comfort level, with a mental health professional available on-site. The training included: (1) check-ins and presession survey (10 minutes); (2) a didactic on recognizing mental health warning signs, next steps to support a peer, institution-specific and broader resources, and tips for self-care (35 minutes); (3) a practical scenario-based dyad role-playing exercise with learners taking turns acting as a peer in distress and peer supporter (30 minutes); and (4) Q&A, group discussion, and postsession survey (15 minutes; Table 1).

*Table 1. Peer-to-Peer Mental Health Support Training Overview*

A total of 164 HMS/HSDM Pathways Program students completed the required training on March 29, 2024. In the first portion of the training, the peer leader provided a didactic presentation, which covered signs of mental health distress, the do's and don'ts of how to support peers experiencing mental health concerns, how to access resources (institution-specific, local, and national), and self-care strategies. The didactic presentation was interactive, with brainstorms and discussions for learners to share signs of peer distress and strategies for providing support. Key mental health and wellness resources, both on and off campus, were discussed, referencing the mental health and wellness one-page handouts the task force created, which included key institution-specific, local, and national resources.

In the second portion of the training, learners paired up for role-plays to practice responding to a distressed peer. Each individual received a written dyad role-playing scenario (Appendix D—includes all scenarios, updated and adapted for general use) describing a theoretical yet realistic HMS/HSDM student's experience with navigating a specific mental health challenge. Participants took turns as actors and peer supporters, applying the skills covered earlier in the training. This allowed learners to experience both roles, receive real-time feedback from their peers, and reflect on what was most helpful and what could be improved. Two suggested scenarios were provided, along with an alternate option for those who preferred a different topic. Learners were encouraged to inform their trainers and/or step out if they felt uncomfortable participating in the role-playing exercises.

In the final portion of the training, learners returned to the larger group to reflect on key takeaways, ask final questions, and complete the postsession survey. For any concerns or questions beyond their peer leaders’ comfort, learners were referred to an on-site psychiatrist from the university health service, who was available during and after the session. The study was reviewed by the HMS Program in Medical Education Educational Scholarship Review Committee and deemed to be Educational Quality Improvement and therefore exempt from institutional review board review.

### Training Logistics

Eight rooms equipped with audiovisual technology were reserved for the small-group sessions, allowing for the presentation of slides. A staff psychiatrist was available for student questions during and after the session in a separate location within the same building. Peer leaders also had access to whiteboards for use during the brainstorming exercises, which took place before each major section of the didactic portion (signs of distress, do's and don'ts, and resources).

### Pre- and Postsession Surveys

The effectiveness of the training session was assessed using pre- and postsession surveys (Appendix E) that measured learners’ confidence in supporting peers with mental health concerns, practicing self-care, and accessing mental health resources. Surveys also evaluated knowledge on identifying signs of distress, appropriate actions, self-care, and resources, including a question on how to support peers with suicidal ideation. The survey items were developed by multiple team members, including student task force members and a faculty expert.

Each of the eight confidence items (e.g., question 3: “How comfortable do you feel identifying signs of mental health distress?”) was rated on a 5-point Likert scale by the learner (1 = not comfortable, 3 = somewhat comfortable, 5 = very comfortable). For the three discrete knowledge items (e.g., question 11: “Talking with a peer about suicide can increase their suicidal ideation and chance of suicide completion”), learners indicated whether the statement was true or false. For the three scenario-based items, learners were given a scenario describing a peer with signs of mental health distress and were asked to indicate the appropriate response from among four possible responses (e.g., question 14: “Which answer best describes the peer's signs of mental health distress?”). The postsession survey asked learners to identify the most and least helpful sections and provided space for open-ended feedback. Learners used an anonymous eight-digit identifier for data matching, composed of their birth day/month and the last four digits of their phone number, with only a few student leaders having access to individual responses.

### Data Analysis

A total of 97 students responded to the confidence items and 96 responded to the knowledge items on the pre- and postsession surveys, and these responses were successfully matched for analysis. The survey was delivered to learners in an online format via Qualtrics XM. Results were assessed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 29.0.0.0. Analysis based on Cronbach's alpha indicated that the survey scale was highly reliable (presession α = .87; postsession α = .94).

For items assessing learner confidence, a paired t test using a two-sided significance cutoff of p < .05 was employed to compare each item on the pre- and postsession surveys. For items assessing learner knowledge, first a numeric value was assigned to represent whether the selected answer was correct (0 = incorrect, 1 = correct). A sum score of knowledge, with 6 being the maximum, was then computed, representing the total number of questions correctly answered by each learner. Thereafter, a paired t test using a two-sided significance cutoff of p < .05 was employed to compare both the sum score and the individual scores for the knowledge assessment questions on the pre- and postsession surveys. Cohen's d was calculated to determine effect size for all t tests. The qualitative data were gathered through both multiple-choice and open-ended questions on the same survey; number of responses per multiple-choice question/answer pairing was computed automatically through Qualtrics XM.

## Results

One hundred sixty-four HMS/HSDM students completed the required training in March 2024.

### Quantitative Findings

#### Confidence items

A paired t test for each of the eight items assessing learner confidence was conducted to compare the mean learner scores before and after the training session. We observed a statistically significant increase in mean score for all eight confidence items after the training as compared to before the training, indicative of increased learner confidence after the training. Details are provided in Table 2.

*Table 2. Mean Difference in Confidence Items Among All Matched Participants (N = 97)*

#### Knowledge items

A paired t test for each of the six items assessing learner knowledge, as well as a sum score of learner knowledge, was conducted to compare the mean learner scores before and after the training session. We observed a statistically significant increase in the sum score of knowledge after the training as compared to before the training (mean of 5.6 versus 5.4 [p = .04], mean difference of 0.16 [95% CI, 0.01–0.31]), indicative of increased learner knowledge after the training. Interestingly, the percentage of learners selecting the desired response to a knowledge question was statistically significantly increased after the training as compared to before the training only for the self-care statement: “Self-care is important, but our responsibility to our peers and patients should be prioritized over all else” (desired answer false; mean score of 0.91 versus 0.85 [p = .03], mean difference of 0.05 [95% CI, 0.01–0.10]). Details are provided in Table 3.

*Table 3. Mean Difference in Knowledge Items Among All Matched Participants (N = 96)*

### Qualitative Findings

Overall, learners appreciated the peer-to-peer format, the safe learning environment, and the provided foundation for peer support. Learners reported mixed feelings on the timing of the session during the middle of the academic year. About half of the students who responded to the survey agreed that the timing was optimal, with some claiming they felt sufficiently comfortable with their classmates at this point in the year to engage in these sorts of discussions. However, about the same number of students stated that the training would have been a helpful experience earlier in their academic year, particularly during orientation. Learners indicated that it was helpful to be divided into small groups within their academic societies, with each group comprising approximately 45 medical and dental students who engage in case-based learning throughout the majority of their preclinical training at HMS/HSDM.

Both learners and peer leaders suggested incorporating guidance on setting boundaries during emotionally intense conversations with peers. Additionally, students expressed a need for clearer information about the university's urgent care line, including its function and implications for personal mental health support or assisting a peer. Lastly, some students reported discomfort asking questions directly to the on-site mental health professional and preferred an anonymous option.

### Other Measures

Students reported that the three most helpful sections of the session were the do's and don'ts of how to support peers (n = 31, 32%), the mental health resources/Counseling and Mental Health Service videos (n = 25, 26%), and the paired dyad practice scenarios (n = 17, 18%); however, some learners found these same sessions to not be helpful. The three sections of the session reported to be least helpful were self-care (n = 34, 35%), paired dyad practice scenarios (n = 19, 20%), and mental health resources/Counseling and Mental Health Service videos (n = 18, 19%).

## Discussion

Medical and dental students face significantly higher rates of depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation than the general population.1,25 An interactive, institution-specific mental health training session that incorporates skills practice with feedback helps to prepare students to support one another and themselves. The peer-driven approach with support from administration and mental health experts is paramount, fostering open conversations about sensitive topics led by those with shared experiences. Pre- and postsession survey results support the effectiveness of this approach as foundational training for all incoming medical and dental students, with significantly improved confidence in all assessed areas and significant improvement in demonstrated knowledge highlighted by the improved sum score of all knowledge questions. With a greater knowledge base and confidence in this arena, the results suggest that engaging in this training may allow students to be better prepared to support both themselves and their peers prior to an acute mental health crisis, particularly through an improvement in their understanding of self-care as well as their comfort with identifying signs of mental health distress and appropriately responding to a distressed peer.

Despite high rates of psychological distress, medical and dental students often hesitate to disclose mental health concerns due to stigma, fear of repercussions, lack of support, and concerns about licensing.26–29 Studies have demonstrated that many learners fear professional repercussions and judgment from peers and faculty, which can deter them from seeking timely support. Our training aims to normalize discussions around mental health and peer support, potentially mitigating these barriers by fostering an environment where students can openly engage in conversations led by peers who share similar experiences.

There are several limitations to the study. Although matched anonymous pre- and postsession surveys showed significant improvements in confidence and overall knowledge, no statistically significant increase was observed in the number of desired responses to individual knowledge questions, except for the self-care question. This discrepancy could be attributed to the study design, as the pre-then-post questionnaire design can predispose to response shift bias, in which participants use a different frame of understanding to answer each survey.30 Additionally, the high baseline percentage of correct responses (80%–90%) on the presession survey likely contributed to the lack of statistically significant improvement. Our assessment strategy was also partially limited by its reliance on self-reported confidence gains rather than an objective skills assessment, and the usage of open-ended questions as qualitative data.31 On the one hand, open-ended questions offer an opportunity to elaborate on closed-ended responses and identify new concerns. On the other hand, time burden, negativity bias, and respondent demographics may impact the likelihood of responding to open-ended questions, leading to potentially skewed data.31,32 Future studies should consider utilizing a post-then-pre questionnaire model to reduce response shift bias and incorporate objective skills assessments alongside self-reported measures to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of participants’ knowledge and abilities.30

When determining the session's length, the goal was to balance providing high-yield information with allowing students time to practice peer-support skills, while staying within the 90-minute time slot that the curriculum permitted. A longer session (e.g., 2 hours) could allow more time for practicing peer-support skills through the dyads, more time for discussing self-care in greater detail, and a better pacing overall. Separately, this training may have limited applicability to other settings due to differences in institutional context and availability of support resources, limited or no opportunities for inclusion during the first-year curriculum, and limited availability of senior peer trainers and current students interested in becoming peer leaders. Our peer leaders were given the freedom to use the presentation slides as a baseline structure and encouraged to make it their own, adding and emphasizing the points they found to be most useful, which may have led to significant intertrainer variability. Grouping students by academic societies, where they have already established rapport, facilitated engagement and may be a helpful approach for schools with similar structures. At Harvard, medical and dental students are largely taught in the same classroom during their first year, making a small-group training more feasible than at other institutions. Lastly, although the workshop evaluation was created by multiple students and a faculty advisor with strong backgrounds in mental health, it was not based on a singular educational theory and did not use a previously validated evaluation tool.

Although the training was successful in achieving its overall goals, several lessons have emerged that may help colleagues seeking to adapt the training to their own institution. Smaller groups and/or multiple pairs of peer leaders per group could be considered, depending on interest and availability. In addition to limiting access to the raw survey data, in the future randomly generated unique codes could be assigned as anonymous identifiers rather than using components of students’ birthdays and phone numbers, in order to optimally safeguard privacy and minimize the risk of noncompliance with FERPA and/or HIPAA regulations. Some peer leaders made time for an icebreaker at the beginning of the session. Many learners found this helpful to open up the discussion, and we are planning to systematically integrate this into future presentations. Learners also expressed a need for clearer guidance on setting boundaries in emotionally intense conversations, which we will incorporate into the do's and don'ts for peer support and the dyad practice sections for future groups.

Furthermore, questions arose regarding the function and implications of the school's urgent care line when personally seeking mental health support or assisting a peer. In response, we are collaborating with university mental health services to clarify these policies. Another key consideration is how mental health professionals are integrated into the session. Some students reported feeling uncomfortable asking questions directly to the on-site mental health professional and preferred an anonymous option. A potential solution is to offer an optional debrief panel after the session, where a mental health professional can address questions submitted anonymously through an online Q&A platform. This approach may help foster a more inclusive and psychologically safe learning environment.

Overall, this training will continue to serve as a foundational part of the HMS/HSDM curriculum for years to come, with leadership responsibility passed on from one class to the next, and the presentation improved yearly based on feedback from all constituents. We hope that our training will serve as a model for other medical and dental schools to adapt to their own contexts so that incoming medical and dental students nationally will have access to peer-led training in mental health, well-being, and peer support as vital aspects of their education.
